Q: How do I deploy a website using a separate CSS stylesheet? A:

Here is the documentation for GitLab Pages, which I'd highly recommend reviewing.

The issue appears to be with your script:

cp -r ./*.* ./public/
  • cp: The copy command
  • -r: Recursive option to also look in child directories
  • ./*.*: Look in the current directory (./) for any file with a dot in it (*.*)
  • ./public/: Copy the matched files to the public folder.

This will certainly match assets/css/style.css because style.css has a dot in the filename, but it would literally copy the file to the public folder. Instead, you want to copy every from your current directory into the public folder so that it keeps your file structure.

There is one caveat, and it is detailed in the documents page referenced above:

Then the .gitlab-ci.yml example below moves all files from the root directory of the project to the public/ directory. The .public workaround is so cp doesn’t also copy public/ to itself in an infinite loop:

script:
  - mkdir .public
  - cp -r * .public
  - mv .public public

Q: MDX ParallelPeriod returns null (or the wrong total) on All member when querying a year range A:

On the two issues:

  • [All] sits above [Year], so ParallelPeriod() has no relative anchor and returns null.

  • Listing 2007:2010 on Axis 1 dictates display rows, not evaluation context. [All] still represents the entire dimension history.

Solution 1: filterby/subselect

Filter the range in a filterby (icCube-specific) or subselect. This shrinks the active subcube so [All] evaluates strictly over 2007-2010:

WITH 
MEMBER [Measures].[Amount Last Yr] AS
  IIF(
    [Time].[Calendar].CurrentMember IS [Time].[Calendar].[All],
    SUM(
      EXISTING [Time].[Calendar].[Year].Members,
      ([Measures].[Amount], ParallelPeriod([Time].[Calendar].[Year], 1, [Time].[Calendar].CurrentMember))
    ),
    ([Measures].[Amount], ParallelPeriod([Time].[Calendar].[Year], 1, [Time].[Calendar].CurrentMember))
  )

SELECT
  {[Measures].[Amount], [Measures].[Amount Last Yr]} ON 0,
  [Time].[Calendar].[Year].Members + {[Time].[Calendar].[All]} ON 1
FROM [Sales]
FILTERBY [Time].[Calendar].[Year].[2007]:[Time].[Calendar].[Year].[2010]

Solution 2: custom total member

Bypass [All] entirely and create a custom all member:

WITH 
SET [SelectedYears] AS 
  [Time].[Calendar].[Year].[2007]:[Time].[Calendar].[Year].[2010]

MEMBER [Time].[Calendar].[Total Selected] AS 
  SUM([SelectedYears])

MEMBER [Measures].[Amount Last Yr] AS
  IIF(
    [Time].[Calendar].CurrentMember IS [Time].[Calendar].[Total Selected],
    SUM(
      [SelectedYears],
      ([Measures].[Amount], ParallelPeriod([Time].[Calendar].[Year], 1, [Time].[Calendar].CurrentMember))
    ),
    ([Measures].[Amount], ParallelPeriod([Time].[Calendar].[Year], 1, [Time].[Calendar].CurrentMember))
  )

SELECT
  {[Measures].[Amount], [Measures].[Amount Last Yr]} ON 0,
  [SelectedYears] + {[Time].[Calendar].[Total Selected]} ON 1
FROM [Sales]

Q: Grouping by variables in a dataset across multiple columns A:

Convert to long form by stringing out the colors column by column with the associated values (or using reshape). Then calculate the associated aov ANOVA and use emmeans with that to adjust for the unbalanced data.

Finally compare these using Tukey HSD to take the simultaneous inference into account.
p < 0.05 indicates significant difference or looking at the confidence intervals any that does not overlap zero indicates the same.

library(dplyr)
library(emmeans)
 
long <- my_data %>%
  { data.frame(value = .[[1]], color = unlist(.[-1])) }

# or
# long <- reshape(my_data, list(-1), "color", dir = "long")

fm <- aov(value ~ color, long)
em <- emmeans(fm, ~ color)
p <- pairs(em, adjust = "tukey")
print(p)
##  contrast        estimate   SE df t.ratio p.value
##  black - green     -2.433 2.71  7  -0.899  0.8887
##  black - orange    -3.433 2.71  7  -1.268  0.7168
##  black - purple    -5.450 2.97  7  -1.838  0.4236
##  black - red       -2.100 2.97  7  -0.708  0.9481
##  green - orange    -1.000 2.42  7  -0.413  0.9925
##  green - purple    -3.017 2.71  7  -1.114  0.7951
##  green - red        0.333 2.71  7   0.123  0.9999
##  orange - purple   -2.017 2.71  7  -0.745  0.9386
##  orange - red       1.333 2.71  7   0.493  0.9856
##  purple - red       3.350 2.97  7   1.130  0.7876
##
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 5 estimates 

plot(p)

Q: Scan directories and copy those that have more than n files A:

Since OP has commented - I haven't coded for 20 years - and has tagged the question with bash, I'll throw a (relatively) basic bash script into the mix.

First, create OP's sample directories/files:

rm -rf music*

mkdir -p music{,light}

mkdir -p music/artist{1..3}

mkdir -p music/artist1/album{1..3}
touch music/artist1/album1/1-1-1.txt
touch music/artist1/album2/1-2-{1..2}.txt
touch music/artist1/album3/1-3-{1..6}.txt

mkdir -p music/artist2/album1
touch music/artist2/album1/2-1-1.txt

mkdir -p music/artist3/album{1..2}
touch music/artist3/album1/3-1-1.txt
touch music/artist3/album2/3-2-{1..2}.txt

Result:

$ tree
├── music
│   ├── artist1
│   │   ├── album1
│   │   │   └── 1-1-1.txt
│   │   ├── album2
│   │   │   ├── 1-2-1.txt
│   │   │   └── 1-2-2.txt
│   │   └── album3
│   │       ├── 1-3-1.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-2.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-3.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-4.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-5.txt
│   │       └── 1-3-6.txt
│   ├── artist2
│   │   └── album1
│   │       └── 2-1-1.txt
│   └── artist3
│       ├── album1
│       │   └── 3-1-1.txt
│       └── album2
│           ├── 3-2-1.txt
│           └── 3-2-2.txt
├── musiclight

11 directories, 15 files

General design:

  • use find / type -d to obtain a list of artists (directories)
  • for each artist use find / type -f to obtain a list of songs (files) under the artist's directory
  • to get around potential issues with file names containing linefeeds or control characters we'll have find just print a 1 (ie, we don't care about file names at this point so we just need something simple we can count)
  • use wc -l to count the results of the 2nd find (ie, the number of songs/files)
  • if the count is greater-than/equal to OP's threshold (eg, threshold=7) then recursively copy the artist's directory to the target directory

Putting all of this into bash code:

src='music'
tgt='musiclight'

threshold=7

while read -r artist
do
    [[ "${artist}" == "${src}" ]] && continue                  # ignore top most directory '${src}'

    song_count=$(find "${artist}" -type f -printf '1\n' | wc -l)

    if [[ "${song_count}" -ge "${threshold}" ]]
    then
        cp -rp "${artist}" "${tgt}"                            # recursively copy files, preserve mode/ownership/timestamps
    fi
done< <(find "${src}" -maxdepth 1 -type d)                     # get list of artists

NOTE: while the find / -type f snippet addresses potential file names with embedded linefeeds, the find / -type d snippet does not address potential directory names with embedded linefeeds; if the latter is an issue for OP we can come back and look at an additional edit

Result for threshold=7:

$ tree musiclight
musiclight
└── artist1
    ├── album1
    │   └── 1-1-1.txt
    ├── album2
    │   ├── 1-2-1.txt
    │   └── 1-2-2.txt
    └── album3
        ├── 1-3-1.txt
        ├── 1-3-2.txt
        ├── 1-3-3.txt
        ├── 1-3-4.txt
        ├── 1-3-5.txt
        └── 1-3-6.txt

4 directories, 9 files

Result for threshold=3:

musiclight

│   ├── album1

Q: What can the dot command repeat, exactly? A:

In Vim, . repeats the last change made to the buffer. It repeats editing commands such as insert, delete, change, replace, paste, indent, and similar modifications. It does not repeat normal motions like w or j, or : commands. For more complex sequences involving movement and changes, use a macro such as qa...q and replay it with @a.
